title: Betrayal: Make Every Defender a Blocker
summary: Drive the king with pawn checks, then sacrifice the rook so Black’s own bishop closes its last escape.

nodes.question: How can White continue when the queen and bishop still defend the king?
nodes.explanation: h4+ forces Kf5. Then g4+ forces the h-pawn onto g4, and Rf4+ forces the bishop onto f4. Those black pieces become barriers when e4 delivers mate.

nodes.question: What can we learn from the separate pawn ending?
nodes.explanation: White’s active king supports the central pawn. The independent g3/Kf5/e4+ line controls f4 before advancing with check; the exact seven-piece positions remain winning for White.

branches.title: Source finish: force the defenders into the cage
commentary: Begin after ...Kg5 in the complete later diagram. White must use checks to keep Black’s queen and bishop from taking over.
h4+ checks the king with the pawn from h2. Kd5 covers e4 and e5, Rb4 controls the fourth rank, and Black’s own pieces restrict its king.
Kf5 is the sole legal reply. White has driven the king toward the square attacked by a future e4 pawn advance, but must first remove an escape resource.
g4+ checks f5 with the g-pawn. It offers that pawn to the black h5 pawn and begins filling the king’s lower escape squares with its own army.
hxg4 is the sole legal reply. Black’s pawn on g4 now blocks that square for its own king; White’s surviving h4 pawn controls g5.
Rf4+ sacrifices the rook directly beside the king. The queen on f6 cannot move down through its own king on f5 to capture it.
Bxf4 is the sole legal reply. The bishop leaves h6 and now occupies f4, another square that Black’s king will need.
e4# checks f5. Kd5 protects e4 and controls e5/e6; Qf6, Bf4 and the g4/g6 pawns block four more flights, while h4 controls g5. The defenders have become the king’s cage.

branches.title: Independent practice from the source pawn ending
commentary: This separate seven-piece source diagram is a different variation. It is not reached by joining it onto the larger mating line.
g3 controls f4 and h4 before the central pawn advances. White keeps an exact win with all five pawns retained.
Kf5 is a representative legal Black reply. The king approaches the central pawn, but f4 is now controlled by g3.
e4+ advances with check, supported by Kd5. White uses king activity and the supporting pawn instead of rushing an unsupported pawn race.
Kg5 is a representative retreat. The branch stops at a tablebase-checked White win; the remaining conversion and other Black replies are not presented as forced moves.

exercises.prompt: Why offer the rook instead of immediately pushing e4?
exercises.answer: In the verified plan, Rf4+ forces the bishop onto f4. When e4 checks next, that bishop blocks a king flight instead of defending from a distance.

exercises.prompt: What does g3 contribute before e4+?
exercises.answer: It controls f4. That removes a king retreat when the central pawn advances, while Kd5 supports e4.
